    name: Dossier generation
    path: 00_System/skills/dossier-generation.md
    instructions: "Uses: answer\n\nWrite the actual dossier in Markdown. Do not describe
      how to write it, return a\nplan, or replace the document with a link. These
      instructions govern dossier\nwriting only. The supporting skills remain independent.
      Use their relevant\nreasoning and source guidance; this document's purpose and
      structure take\nprecedence over their chat-only formats, intake prompts, and
      stopping rules.\nDo not run new research merely to refresh the dossier.\n\n##
      Purpose\n\nGive counsel an editable, current view of the whole matter across
      any area of\nlaw. Use the supplied matter records and saved research. Lead with
      the answer\nand the judgment needed. Be concise but retain the reasoning a lawyer
      needs.\nDo not add generic disclaimers or turn missing support into a refusal.\n\nThe
      North Star is the business's controlling question and objective, starting\nwith
      the original request and any explicit lawyer clarification or reframe.\nThe
      latest chat question is normally a supporting inquiry, not replacement\nscope.
      Answer the business question even when a later exchange is narrow.\nTest the
      premise behind the request. Explain when the evidence supports a\ndifferent
      answer, a changed route, or not proceeding. Do not force the facts\nto support
      the business's proposed solution or silently rewrite its question.\n\nAssess
      material issues from the current records and relevant history across\nall supplied
      matter conversations. The saved issue list is a starting point,\nnot a ceiling.
      Include a newly identified material issue in the Issues section,\nwith its source
      and effect on the business question. Use ordinary headings for\nissues without
      saved IDs; do not invent an ID or claim the issue list was changed.\nRead omitted
      passages through the captured-record reader when needed. Preserve\ntheir speaker,
      date, corrections and hypothetical scope. Do not claim that\navailable records
      were all read. Judge detail by its value to the business\nanswer and counsel's
      next decision, not a fixed depth-versus-breadth quota.\n\nOn a refresh, derive
      the current position again from the current records and\nsupported issue analysis.
      The prior dossier is fallible synthesis for continuity,\nnot a wording template
      or evidence that an activity is cleared. Keep useful\nreasoning, but replace
      conclusions and assumption labels that the current inputs\ndo not support. Preserve
      the recorded direction and decisions as records; explain\nseparately when this
      draft recommends a change. Retention of prior research means\nit stays accessible,
      not that its earlier conclusions must stay unchanged.\n\nWrite the general matter
      dossier, even when the conversation is exploring an\nalternative. The current
      direction stays the planning baseline. Recording a\nhypothetical in this document
      does not adopt it or change any reported fact.\n\n## Reading order\n\n1. A short
      title and **Current position**: answer the business question in a\n   short
      decision brief. Give the recommended course now, why it best serves\n   the
      objective, what can proceed, and what should wait or change. Name the\n   decisive
      conditions, not every information gap. Distinguish this draft's\n   recommendation
      from the accepted working view and any recorded decision.\n2. **Decision question**:
      reproduce the supplied controlling business question exactly. It\n   is the
      matter's scope, not a question for the model to replace.\n   If no question
      has been recorded, frame a provisional business question from\n   the original
      request; do not substitute the latest conversational subquestion.\n3. One **Issues**
      section covering EVERY supplied issue. Keep each issue's\n   stable identity
      with an invisible `<!-- issue:ISS-... -->` marker before its\n   heading. Do
      not substitute a second, different issue list.\n4. **Next actions**: a short,
      ranked work plan. For each action give the\n   deliverable, the result needed
      to proceed, the dependent decision or activity,\n   and the fallback if that
      result is not available. Order by dependencies and\n   time sensitivity, not
      merely the saved issue order. Reuse assigned work and\n   its recorded owner
      and date. When no assignment exists, suggest an owner\n   role and timing relative
      to a real milestone, clearly labeled **Proposed**.\n   Do not invent a person,
      commitment, legal deadline, or calendar date.\n   Distinguish a source-based
      deadline from a suggested working target.\n5. Brief links to available current
      work product, supporting records, and prior\n   revisions. Omit empty inventories
      and routine record housekeeping that does\n   not affect the decision. Do not
      paste the old dossier or superseded advice\n   into the body.\n\n## Each issue\n\nDefault
      to a compact CRAC structure: **Current answer**, **Rule and support**,\n**Application**,
      and **Next step**. The last part states the practical effect,\nnot a repetition
      of the opening. Use CREAC when interpreting the authority\nneeds a separate
      **Explanation**. Use IRAC only when the issue itself still\nneeds to be framed.
      Do not pad a section to meet a template.\n\nKeep work status separate from the
      legal answer. Show what remains: information,\nresearch, analysis, a decision,
      or implementation. A supplied answer to a fact\nquestion does not by itself
      close the legal issue. Keep answered questions with\nthe facts they establish,
      rather than in the open-question list.\n\nRetain prior analysis of issues untouched
      by the latest research. Say when an\nissue has not been researched or when changed
      inputs may affect its prior view.\nDepth on one issue must not make the other
      issues disappear.\n\nGive each issue one useful current answer, even without
      completed research.\nExplain the likely result, the facts or rule it depends
      on, and the next useful\ncheck. Do not give only a referral to legal or say
      merely that research is needed.\nMake the reasoning usable: identify the applicable
      actor, conduct, jurisdiction\nor contract, and the operative test. Apply each
      decisive condition to the known\nfacts. If a material fact is missing, explain
      the result on either side of that\nfact and recommend an interim course. A statement
      that something 'depends on\nthe terms' is incomplete unless it says which term
      matters and how it changes\nthe answer. Address a material exception or competing
      reading when it could\nchange the recommendation; do not invent one to fill
      a template.\n\nUse saved source passages to explain the rule and its material
      qualifications,\nwith the source and locator beside the proposition. A source
      title, URL, or\nopening excerpt alone is not the operative rule. Treat private
      agreements and\ncompany policies as those types of support, not public law.
      If no relevant\nauthority is saved, give the best conditional analysis and label
      that legal\npremise as unverified. State the precise research question once;
      do not repeat\n'not researched' in place of analysis or claim research happened
      in this run.\n\nConnect issues that affect the same decision. Explain what a
      proposed mitigation\nsolves, what it does not solve, and which dependency must
      be met first. Distinguish\na legal requirement from a recommended risk control
      or business preference.\nA possible way forward is not permission to proceed.
      Separating activities or\nmilestones does not establish that either is cleared;
      qualify the earlier step\nwhen its independent contractual or legal conditions
      are not established.\nThe application places full saved research in a disclosure
      under its issue;\ndo not create saved-research disclosures yourself, repeat
      old analysis, or add a\nsaved-answer appendix. Write the current synthesis;
      the application preserves\nthe original research separately.\n\n## Alternatives
      considered\n\nInclude this section when saved alternatives are supplied. Use
      one subsection\nper alternative, with its `<!-- alternative:SCN-... -->` marker
      and saved title.\nLabel it **Hypothetical — not adopted** (or archived, if the
      record says so).\nState its assumptions, how it helps or hinders the objective,
      added risks,\nissues it leaves unresolved, and the next action. Keep each alternative's\nworking
      note and attached test evidence within that alternative. Do not blend\nseparate
      proposals or treat a test assumption as an actual matter fact.\nInclude material
      dates, controls, and dependencies from the saved working note.\nLink the saved
      alternative. Do not infer acceptance or a recorded decision.\nFor each decisive
      condition, explain what the alternative changes and what still\napplies. A change
      in format, asset, actor, or channel does not itself remove a\npermission requirement
      or contractual restriction. If the saved terms do not\nsettle whether the restriction
      applies to the alternative, state that condition.\nDo not present uncertain
      exemption as the reason the fallback can proceed.\nCompare viable alternatives
      with the current direction on the factors that\nactually change the choice,
      such as timing, scope, cost, and unresolved risk.\nRecommend when to use each
      option. Do not give an unranked menu or assume that a\nfallback solves unrelated
      issues. New options proposed in this draft are not\nsaved alternatives, selected
      directions, or commitments.\n\n## Record and source distinctions\n\n- Take requester-supplied
      facts as reported facts. Do not demote them to model\n  assumptions merely because
      they were not independently verified. Flag a\n  material inconsistency when
      the records actually conflict.\n- Reconcile newer reported answers with older
      assumptions and open questions.\n  Check that material counts, dates, and totals
      agree. State the conflict and\n  its effect when they do not; do not silently
      choose a convenient value.\n  Check simple arithmetic and chronology when a
      conclusion depends on them.\n  Compare metadata with reported milestones. Put
      each material unresolved\n  inconsistency in **Record conflicts**, with the
      practical effect and the fact\n  needed to resolve it. Preserve the reported
      values; do not correct the record\n  or omit the inconsistency merely because
      the rest of the analysis can proceed.\n- Test the legal premise of an issue
      title. Name the relevant actor and explain\n  why a duty applies to that actor.
      Do not extend a rule to a different class\n  of entity without a basis, or treat
      every missing record as a breach. Where legal access to\n  sensitive records
      is restricted, distinguish permitted diligence from an\n  instruction to disclose
      or transfer the restricted material.\n- Keep model assumptions separate. State
      only those actually used and explain\n  which conclusion depends on them. Unknown
      facts remain unknown. Do not list\n  reported facts, resolved old assumptions,
      or things not assumed in this section.\n  An earlier assumption label does not
      override a later reported fact.\n- A missing record proves a record gap, not
      the absence of a right, approval,\n  consent, or obligation. Do not turn \"not
      saved\" into \"does not exist\" or a\n  categorical legal prohibition. Do not
      present an inferred business activity\n  as supplied fact. When a conclusion
      depends on unknown facts or applicable\n  law, state that condition and give
      the next useful check.\n- Distinguish a proposed view, the accepted working
      view, and an explicitly\n  recorded decision. Generating this document records
      no new decision.\n- Use the current direction's working note as fallible analysis,
      not facts.\n  Keep unresolved or stale findings qualified. Reconcile old dossier
      and research\n  assumptions against current records in the current answer; do
      not repeat a\n  superseded premise merely because preserved research still contains
      it.\n- Link support beside the claim it supports. Preserve supplied, retrieved,\n
      \ read, and verified source distinctions. Retrieval is not proof of support.\n
      \ An earlier model answer is not legal authority. Do not invent citations.\n-
      Use current support labels. Do not repeat an old 'no sources retrieved'\n  statement
      when the current record contains sources. State the actual gap.\n\nThe application
      retains version history and checks for concurrent changes.\nReturn the useful
      document even when some support or optional structure is\nunavailable. Do not
      change facts, issue status, recommendations, or decisions."

    supporting_skills:
    - skill_id: answer
      path: 00_System/experimental-chat/answer.md
      instructions: 'For substantive legal answers, use a visible legal reasoning
        structure. Choose it from the dialogue; never ask the lawyer to select a writing
        format.


        Default to IRAC when the lawyer is exploring, asks to understand more, has
        not chosen a path, or may not yet know the legal question. Frame the question
        for the lawyer rather than assuming legal knowledge. Use these exact bold
        labels, each starting a separate short paragraph:


        **Issue** — State the legal question in plain language and why it matters
        to this matter.


        **Rule** — Explain the relevant rule. Link support beside the proposition
        it supports. If you can reliably name a relevant authority that has not been
        retrieved or verified, show its name or citation beside the proposition with
        **Needs checking**, following the research skill. State what remains unverified;
        do not substitute a generic absence-of-sources notice for a known source lead.


        **Analysis** — Connect the specific facts to the rule. Explain the material
        competing interpretation or missing fact if there is one. This must be reasoning,
        not a repeated rule or bare conclusion.


        **Conclusion** — Give the provisional view and the next useful point to explore.
        A recommendation is optional; understanding comes first.


        Switch to CRAC once the lawyer has chosen a path or requests a focused answer
        to a clear question. Use **Conclusion**, **Rule**, **Analysis**, and **Conclusion
        / next step**, in that order. The last section gives the practical implication
        or next step rather than repeating the opening. A request for a quick answer
        does not by itself establish that the issue is clear; keep IRAC if framing
        is still needed. If the lawyer returns to exploring or is confused, return
        to IRAC.


        For a focused answer that needs interpretation of authorities, use CREAC:
        **Conclusion**, **Rule**, **Explanation**, **Analysis**, **Conclusion / next
        step**. Explanation describes how supported authorities interpret the rule;
        Analysis applies that interpretation to this matter. Do not invent examples,
        cases, or support to fill a section.


        For a single legal question, make these reasoning labels visible. Let the
        explanation determine section length; use the dialogue skill’s flexible reading-time
        guide without reducing analysis to unexplained labels. Cover the question
        asked, including material alternatives and support limits. For a comparison,
        use the comparison format below instead of repeating a legal-answer template
        for each option. Simple acknowledgments, intake questions, document-type questions,
        and operational updates do not need a legal-answer structure. Preserve the
        initial map format below and existing document templates.


        Distinguish the model''s inference from what a source states. Never invent
        a citation or treat an unsupported preliminary view as settled law. Briefly
        identify when new information changes a prior view and dependent work. Keep
        the explanation the lawyer requested in chat. Create a separate draft when
        the lawyer asks for a document or reusable deliverable; length alone is not
        a reason to move the answer out of the conversation. A decision tree is generated
        only when requested; unknown conditions remain unknown.



        After the lawyer submits intake answers or asks to explore with gaps left
        open, give an initial issue map immediately. Keep it provisional and concise.
        Use a short Markdown section titled "Initial issue map" with a few issue bullets.
        For each, name the likely relevant law or legal framework, explain its connection
        to these facts, and link available supporting authority next to the claim.
        Distinguish verified authority from supplied sources or unverified leads;
        never invent a citation. Briefly identify unknown facts that could change
        the map. Do not treat an unsupported preliminary view as settled law.


        Immediately below the map, include a separate visible section titled "Assumptions
        used". List only the material assumptions used in this analysis, separate
        from facts supplied by the lawyer. For each assumption, briefly say which
        issue, research direction, or conclusion depends on it; put those with the
        greatest effect first. If none are needed, say "No additional assumptions
        used." Keep unknown facts unknown. Do not promote an assumption to a confirmed
        fact, infer its opposite from its removal, or treat acceptance for exploration
        as factual confirmation. Preserve hypothetical scope. These sections are ordinary
        visible prose, not hidden metadata, an editable form, or a mandatory approval
        step.


        After the initial map and assumptions, stop. The chat interface presents three
        next-step controls: Get a quick answer with support, Explore the affected
        laws, and Create a document. Do not duplicate these choices in prose or ask
        the lawyer to manage tools or research runs. Do not create clickable map items
        or assumption controls. For later exploration, answer the selected issue directly
        and update the map or assumptions only when something material changes; do
        not repeat the entire map each turn.


        When the lawyer selects a next step, use the saved intake and conversation
        without repeating intake or the full issue map. For a quick answer, use the
        IRAC or CRAC selection rule above, keep it concise, put source links beside
        supported claims, and state material unknowns. For affected laws, start with
        the most material issue and explain the rule and its application in bite-sized
        steps. Retrieve support when needed; never describe a failed search as successful
        research. If a research attempt fails, give the useful available answer with
        its support limits and a concrete recovery choice. For document creation,
        use the draft skill and existing templates; ask for the document type or audience
        only if unclear. These choices start work, not recorded legal decisions.



        ## Comparing alternatives


        Apply this format to comparisons instead of IRAC. Use about two minutes of
        reading per alternative as a flexible guide, not a hard limit or required
        length. Spend the words on causal explanation, not a catalogue of labels.


        1. State what the company wants to do in concrete terms and the decision this
        comparison informs. Use its product, activity, people, place and timing where
        material. Distinguish the company’s different milestones and do not assume
        they can occur independently without checking relevant dependencies.

        2. Describe each option briefly. Use **Benefits**, **Trade-offs and added
        risks**, and **Issues that remain** as separate paragraph labels. Benefits
        explain how the option advances the company’s objective. Trade-offs and added
        risks explain what the option makes harder or worse, relative to the stated
        baseline, and why. Issues that remain are existing problems the option does
        not solve. Leaving a problem unresolved is not the same as causing or worsening
        it. Do not use “How it hinders” as a catch-all for both. Do not invent a benefit
        or disadvantage to fill a section; say briefly when none is established. A
        new contract is not itself a disadvantage: explain what benefit depends on
        its terms and what happens if it cannot be agreed or implemented in time.
        A risk must identify the proposed activity it affects and the resulting choice
        or constraint.

        3. Explain the material problems that remain under BOTH options. Carry existing
        unresolved issues from the matter into the assessment. Say whether the alternative
        resolves, changes, transfers or leaves each material issue open, and what
        supports that assessment. If an option also worsens an existing issue, distinguish
        that added effect from the unresolved baseline. Explain shared issues once
        where possible, while making clear that they remain under each option. Do
        not assume moving an activity resolves inherited or independent obligations.
        Explain the consequence of an unresolved issue for the company''s plan, not
        just “review X.”

        4. Give a supported tradeoff and the next evidence that could change the choice.
        An earlier assistant recommendation is not an instruction or verified support.
        Reassess both options; do not prefer the current option merely because it
        is current or the alternative has unknowns. If the facts do not support a
        winner, say what determines the choice.


        Use plain, specific language throughout. Do not write “confirm authority,”
        “establish its authority,” “licensing determination,” or “regulatory exposure”
        without explaining the actual activity and legal question. For example, identify
        the proposed activity and whether it needs a license, approval, contractual
        permission or another legal basis, as relevant to this matter. Do not assume
        which basis applies. Explain whether the answer changes where, when or how
        it can provide that service. Define abbreviations when they obscure the point.
        Keep supplied facts, hypothetical assumptions and your inferences distinct.
        Read relevant source passages when needed; label unverified legal treatment
        and do not invent support.


        Before returning the answer, check that a lawyer can tell what the company
        plans to do, how each option affects that plan, why each claimed advantage
        or disadvantage matters, and which existing issues remain. Replace any disconnected
        shorthand with that explanation. Do not add a separate verification step or
        agent.


        Prefer labeled paragraphs for substantial explanation; use tables for compact
        entries. Put each standalone section label at the start of its own paragraph
        with a blank line before and after it. End a bullet list before the next section
        label.

        '

  raw_output: '# Harbor 2 — Mosaic Relay / Harbor Pay acquisition migration


    Matter MAT-20260909-d89ad8 · prepared from the captured records through Sept 10,
    2026 · draft for counsel review


    ## Current position


    **Yes. Four parts of the migration need legal review before the Nov 15 close,
    and each of the four gates day-1 migration. A fifth item gates the close+1 campaign
    launch.** The plan as described is not a data migration. It moves 252,000 customer
    relationships (240k consumer, 12k business) into Mosaic Relay''s app, transfers
    an unreviewed BSA/AML book, and turns Harbor''s license footprint into an assumed,
    rather than verified, four-state expansion.


    The recommended course is to keep the Nov 15 close date and run the four gates
    in parallel, while limiting day-1 onboarding to what Mosaic can lawfully serve:


    | Gate | What it blocks | Milestone |

    |---|---|---|

    | Licensing in Harbor-only states | Onboarding customers there; the bonus campaign
    there | Day 1 / close+1 |

    | KYC reliance for the pre-2023 cohort | The "no re-verification" plan for those
    users | Day 1 |

    | Review of the ~40 open alerts and SAR history | Deal protections; account exclusions
    from the migration book | Before close |

    | Monitoring cutover validation | The day-1 repoint with no coverage gap | Close
    / day 1 |

    | Bonus terms and disclosures | The $50 "Welcome" campaign | Close+1 |


    **Why this serves the objective.** Each gate protects something the deal is buying
    — the license footprint and the customer book — and none of them requires delaying
    the close if work starts now. The riskiest premise in the plan is the one described
    as "a nice win": the four new markets. A combined 44-state footprint is only a
    win if Mosaic can lawfully serve those customers after an **asset purchase**,
    in which Harbor''s licenses stay with Harbor and do not travel with the assets.
    Closing Nov 15 into an unlicensed launch in even a few states, or migrating users
    whose identity records cannot be produced, creates exposure that is difficult
    to unwind after day 1.


    **What can proceed now.** Data mapping and migration engineering; customer notice
    and campaign drafting; monitoring scenario tuning and test runs; the business
    workstreams.


    **What should wait or change.** Onboarding in states where Mosaic lacks a license
    or approval; the bonus launch in those states; treating the alert/SAR review as
    post-close cleanup; and presenting the plan as "no re-verification" until compliance
    confirms that reliance is permitted. SAR content should not travel through the
    ordinary migration data flows.


    **Working view vs. this draft.** The matter already records a working approach:
    treat legal and compliance readiness as a pre-close gate; do not assume Harbor''s
    licenses transfer; consider a narrower launch if licensing, KYC records, alert
    review, or monitoring tests are incomplete (assistant summary, MSG-20260910-2f255e
    — analysis, not a decision). This draft aligns with that approach and specifies
    which item gates which milestone. The material read contains no recorded decision
    on the migration; producing this dossier records none and adopts no alternative.


    **Basis and coverage.** No external authority was retrieved or verified in this
    run, and the 24 captured documents (license schedules, AML/CIP policy, vendor
    contracts, campaign terms) were not read. The saved issue answers and research
    did not arrive with the inputs, so every issue below carries an initial conditional
    answer rather than completed research. Legal propositions name the likely authorities
    and are marked **Needs checking**. Facts are those reported by Dana and the lawyer''s
    intake answers, as recorded in the matter facts file.


    ## Decision question


    > Does any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration need legal review before
    the Nov 15 close?


    Reproduced from the matter record (question ID BQ-c9d7c39f6380eb60). It is the
    matter''s scope and is treated as controlling over any later sub-question.


    ## Issues


    **Issue markers.** The saved issue list was visible in `current-records` only
    in part, and its identifiers were truncated. Headings below use the recorded issue
    titles; no `ISS` markers are attached rather than inventing IDs. Two scope areas
    flagged in the conversation but not confirmed on the saved list are included as
    additional issues with their source noted.


    <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045 -->

    ### Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under the combined
    44-state footprint and whether Harbor''s MTLs transfer/survive the acquisition


    **Current answer** — The premise that Mosaic will "use/assume Harbor''s licenses"
    for the four new markets (lawyer''s intake answer, MSG-20260909-2e549e) is the
    least supportable part of the plan. Money transmission licenses are held by the
    licensee; on an asset purchase they stay with Harbor, and Mosaic needs its own
    authority — or a state-specific successor/transfer mechanism where one exists
    — before it transmits for, or holds balances of, those customers. Provisional
    view: proceed with day-1 migration in states where Mosaic already holds an MTL,
    subject to the other gates; hold the Harbor-only states for licensing or approvals.
    Even in Mosaic-licensed states, confirm that each license covers the specific
    activity for the migrated book (balance holding, business-account features) and
    what filings or notices accompany Harbor''s exit.


    **Rule and support** — State money transmitter statutes require a license to engage
    in money transmission; operating without one can be a federal crime under 18 U.S.C.
    § 1960 as well as a state enforcement matter (**Needs checking** — verify the
    states, the activity, and any exemption). Licenses are generally not transferable
    in an asset sale; states typically require new applications, approvals, or advance
    notice, and many have adopted parts of the Money Transmission Modernization Act
    (**Needs checking**, state by state). A purchase agreement that says licenses
    will "transfer" is a contractual expectation, not the legal permission itself.


    **Application** — On the reported counts (Harbor 38, Mosaic 41, union 44), 35
    states overlap, 3 states are Harbor-only, and 6 are Mosaic-only. The plan''s "four
    new markets" does not match that arithmetic, so the licensing scope cannot be
    sized until both schedules are produced (see Record conflicts). The facts file
    still carries an older assumption that the deal structure was unconfirmed; the
    later explicit answer — asset purchase — controls, which makes non-transfer the
    weak point rather than a bank-style change-of-control filing. Decisive facts:
    the state-by-state license lists; which states allow successor operation and on
    what timeline; and whether Mosaic''s product set for migrated accounts stays inside
    its license permissions.


    **Next step** — Pull both license schedules and build a state matrix with a day-1
    go/no-go column; start applications or approvals immediately, because state processing
    times are the binding constraint against the Nov 15 runway. Interim plan: two-wave
    migration (Mosaic-licensed states on day 1; Harbor-only states after clearance).

    ### BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor''s prior KYC (with missing underlying
    documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay''s independent CIP/AML obligations


    **Current answer** — Mosaic cannot treat Harbor''s pass/fail flags as satisfying
    Mosaic''s own obligations unless its AML/CIP program permits reliance and the
    conditions of that reliance are documented. The lawyer''s intake answer is that
    this is unknown and compliance must confirm — that confirmation is the gating
    item. Provisional view: reliance may be arguable for cohorts whose verification
    records exist and can be transferred; for users onboarded before 2023, whose underlying
    documents were lost when the vendor shut down in 2024, pass/fail flags alone are
    unlikely to evidence verification. Plan to re-verify or step-up verify that cohort,
    or to limit account features until verification is complete. Mosaic should assume
    it bears independent responsibility for each migrated customer, whatever reliance
    its program allows.


    **Rule and support** — AML program requirement, 31 U.S.C. § 5318(h); MSB AML program
    rule, 31 CFR 1022.210 (**Needs checking**). The bank CIP rule, 31 CFR 1020.220,
    contains a reliance provision that requires the other institution to be subject
    to the BSA and regulated by a federal functional regulator, and requires the relying
    institution to obtain and retain the required customer information; whether a
    federal equivalent or a state-MTL requirement governs nonbank money transmitters
    here must be verified (**Needs checking**). Guidance on BSA/AML obligations when
    an institution acquires customer accounts (**Needs checking** — applicability
    to nonbanks).


    **Application** — The 252k users split into cohorts by documentation: records
    for post-2023 onboarding are presumably retrievable; pre-2023 records are not.
    Decisive conditions: the text of Mosaic''s own AML/CIP policy, what the applicable
    state and federal expectations require for reliance, and the size of the missing-document
    cohort (not stated in the records read — obtain the count). Related checks worth
    folding into the same workstream: sanctions-screening evidence for both cohorts,
    and whether beneficial ownership information must be collected or refreshed for
    the 12k business accounts (the federal beneficial ownership requirement for legal
    entity customers, 31 CFR 1010.230, has a defined coverage list — **Needs checking**
    whether it or a state requirement reaches this entity). If reliance is not permitted,
    the options are (a) verify before day 1, (b) migrate with account limits until
    verified, or (c) exclude that cohort from day 1; each choice flows into the migration
    schedule and customer messaging.


    **Next step** — Obtain the AML/CIP policy text and the cohort count from compliance,
    and have compliance with outside AML counsel state in writing whether reliance
    is permitted and on what conditions. That written answer determines the pre-2023
    cohort''s day-1 treatment. Fallback if it is not available before the migration:
    migrate with feature limits and a scheduled verification campaign.

    ### SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage Harbor''s
    ~40 open alerts and SARs


    **Current answer** — This is the item most likely to change the deal or the migration
    list, and it should be reviewed before close through a controlled channel. Read
    all ~40 open alerts and the SAR history; determine whether any implicate accounts
    in the migrated book or reflect ongoing activity that continues past close. Two
    handling constraints apply: SARs and the fact of filing are confidential, so SAR
    content should not be pushed through ordinary migration data flows or shared beyond
    need-to-know personnel; and SARs filed by Harbor do not simply transfer with the
    assets — the acquisition documents should allocate pre-close exposure and post-close
    filing, investigation, and cooperation duties. Provisional view: nothing in the
    record yet suggests a violation — unread alerts are a diligence problem; legal
    risk crystallizes only if required reviews or filings were missed, or continue
    unaddressed after close.


    **Rule and support** — SAR filing duty, 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g)(1); prohibition on
    disclosure, 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g)(2); MSB SAR rule, 31 CFR 1022.320 (**Needs checking**).
    Guidance on how BSA/AML and SAR obligations apply when institutions acquire accounts
    (**Needs checking**).


    **Application** — As of the intake answer, nothing had been reviewed and the alerts
    remained in diligence (MSG-20260909-2e549e). Two practical consequences: once
    read, the alert population becomes an account-level input to the migration list
    — accounts with unresolved suspicion may need exclusion, heightened monitoring,
    or exit; and the review must be structured (clean team / BSA counsel) so SAR information
    is not improperly disclosed to the integration team.


    **Next step** — Stand up the review now. Deliverable: a privileged alert/SAR memo
    with account-level flags and a filing-gap assessment. Fallback if access is delayed:
    negotiate a specific indemnity and cooperation covenant, and keep unresolved accounts
    out of the day-1 book.


    ### Monitoring vendor transition


    **Current answer** — The cutover needs validation before close, not just a repoint
    plan. The reported design — Harbor''s third-party monitoring SaaS contract terminates
    at close; the feed is repointed to Mosaic''s engine on day 1 (FACT-20260909-073838/78d5cd)
    — creates two risks: a coverage gap if the dates do not align, and under-detection
    if Mosaic''s scenarios are not tuned for Harbor''s customer base and typologies
    on day 1. Provisional view: require a documented, tested cutover with a parallel-run
    period, and confirm whether the vendor contract provides post-termination access
    or transition assistance; if not, plan a short extension or interim manual monitoring.


    **Rule and support** — AML program internal controls, 31 U.S.C. § 5318(h) and
    31 CFR 1022.210 (**Needs checking**); the vendor contract''s termination, data-return,
    and transition terms (private contract — read the actual clauses; contract terms
    are support of their own kind, not public law).


    **Application** — The record does not say whether "day 1" is close day or the
    day after; if the contract ends at close and the repoint occurs the next day,
    the record does not say who monitors in between (see Record conflicts). Second,
    tuning: Mosaic''s engine must detect on Harbor''s patterns; a same-day repoint
    without scenario testing can under-detect during the first weeks after close —
    exactly when post-acquisition monitoring matters most.


    **Next step** — Obtain the vendor contract''s termination/data clauses and the
    cutover runbook; require test evidence and a named go/no-go owner before close.
    Fallback: extend Harbor''s vendor through a validated cutover, or dual-run both
    systems briefly.


    ### Welcome bonus campaign ($50 on first transfer, launching close+1)


    **Current answer** — The campaign can likely launch, but not on unreviewed terms
    and not in states where the entity cannot lawfully operate. Review should cover
    the offer mechanics (eligibility, what counts as "first transfer," caps, timing,
    funding); how the bonus posts (a balance credit inside a money-transmission product
    is itself regulated activity and interacts with the unified-balance design); the
    accuracy of advertising claims and required disclosures; and state-by-state availability.
    Provisional view: this is primarily a marketing and disclosure problem, not a
    deal gating item — but it must be tied to the licensing go/no-go list, so a limited-state
    launch may be necessary even if the close date holds.


    **Rule and support** — State UDAP ("little FTC") acts; CFPB UDAAP authority over
    covered persons, Dodd-Frank Act § 1031, 12 U.S.C. § 5531 (**Needs checking** —
    applicability to this entity''s activities). State money-transmission advertising
    and recordkeeping restrictions (**Needs checking**). If any relevant flows are
    transfers to foreign countries, EFTA/Regulation E remittance-transfer disclosure
    and error-resolution duties, 12 CFR part 1005 subpart B (**Needs checking**).
    Tax reporting for the bonus (**Needs checking**).


    **Application** — "First transfer" plus "full access to our product set" means
    the bonus can be earned through a range of product flows, each with its own disclosure
    profile. The decisive inputs are the actual campaign terms and the set of states
    where Mosaic can operate on close+1 — both should be routed to consumer-finance
    review before launch.


    **Next step** — Obtain the campaign brief and terms now; run the review alongside
    the licensing matrix; build a per-state availability check into the launch plan.
    Fallback: launch only in cleared states and hold the rest for a second wave.


    ### Privacy and data protection of the migrated records *(scope area flagged in
    the conversation; not confirmed against the saved issue list)*


    **Current answer** — The transfer of 252k consumer and small-business records
    needs a data-mapping and lawful-basis review before day 1. Likely questions: what
    notices or consents govern moving Harbor''s customer data into Mosaic; what the
    applicable state privacy statutes require for pre-close diligence access and post-close
    processing (notice at collection, opt-outs, limits on onward disclosure); and
    what security and breach-notification exposure follows from records with incomplete
    documentation. Provisional view: the transfer itself can normally be structured
    — several regimes contain merger/asset-sale provisions (**Needs checking**) —
    but notices and data maps should be updated before migration, and Harbor''s customer
    terms may require notice of the transfer.


    **Rule and support** — GLBA privacy and safeguards obligations, 15 U.S.C. §§ 6801–6809;
    Reg P (12 CFR part 1016 / 16 CFR part 313, depending on the enforcing regulator);
    FTC Safeguards Rule, 16 CFR part 314 (**Needs checking** for entity coverage and
    any sale-transfer exception). State comprehensive privacy laws, e.g., California
    CCPA/CPRA (**Needs checking** for each customer state).


    **Application** — The higher-risk element is the combination: incomplete KYC documentation,
    a defunct vendor, and 240k consumer records changing systems. That combination
    raises recordkeeping-integrity and security questions that intersect with the
    KYC issue (can Mosaic evidence verification?) and the account-transfer issue below
    (what the migration looks like to the customer).


    **Next step** — Data inventory and privacy counsel review; fold required notice
    updates into the pre-close communications workstream.


    ### Consumer account transfer mechanics and disclosures *(scope area flagged in
    the conversation; not confirmed against the saved issue list)*


    **Current answer** — Before day 1, confirm the basis on which Harbor''s customer
    relationships move to Mosaic: whether Harbor''s customer agreements permit assignment
    or transfer of the accounts without individual consent, and what disclosures Mosaic
    must deliver (account terms, fee schedule, error-resolution rights, electronic
    consent to new terms). Provisional view: ordinarily solvable with a notice-and-accept
    flow, but it should be designed and reviewed before migration, and it depends
    on the funds-flow decision in the licensing issue (who holds the balance on day
    1).


    **Rule and support** — The customer agreements themselves (private contract);
    E-Sign, 15 U.S.C. § 7001 (**Needs checking**); EFTA/Regulation E where applicable,
    12 CFR part 1005 (**Needs checking**).


    **Application** — "One unified account, one balance, full access to our product
    set" implies new terms and possibly a new account structure at Mosaic. The consent
    mechanics should be sequenced with the KYC plan so the legal bases do not collide
    (a consent flow for new terms is distinct from re-verification, and customer messaging
    should not conflate them).


    **Next step** — Obtain Harbor''s customer agreement and Mosaic''s account terms;
    draft the migration notice and consent flow; review alongside the licensing and
    KYC outputs.


    ## Alternatives considered


    ### Partner bank holds customer funds while Mosaic supplies technology and operations




    **Hypothetical — not adopted.** (Recorded as a comparison path; saved title not
    retrieved, so a descriptive title from the record''s own content is used. The
    record does not show acceptance, and this dossier does not adopt it.)


    **Assumptions** — A bank owns the customer accounts and controls fund movements;
    Mosaic supplies technology and operations. The recorded analysis conditions the
    outcome on that split: the structure "does not automatically remove risk if Mosaic
    controls transfers, owes balances, or acts directly for users" (MSG-20260910-02f34c).


    **How it helps or hinders the objective** — If the bank genuinely owns the accounts
    and controls transfers, this could reduce the money-transmission licensing surface
    ("could lower licensing risk," per the record) and may offer a route to serving
    the new-market states through the bank rather than a Mosaic license. It does not
    remove the KYC, alert, SAR, monitoring, or marketing workstreams — the record
    says those "remain." It adds its own work: bank partnership terms, funds-flow
    mapping, customer-relationship allocation, and a new counterparty — and a bank
    program realistically cannot be contracted and implemented before a Nov 15 day-1
    migration (inference, not a recorded fact).


    **Issues it leaves unresolved** — KYC reliance and missing pre-2023 documentation
    (unchanged — and a partner bank will likely do its own diligence on the same records,
    surfacing the same questions); alerts and SAR handling (unchanged); monitoring
    cutover (unchanged or duplicated at the bank); the bonus terms (unchanged, though
    disclosures may shift). It changes the licensing issue only if the funds flow
    is genuinely bank-owned — a condition the record says must be mapped before any
    assessment.


    **Next action** — Per the record''s own conclusion: map the funds flow, the customer
    relationship, and compliance duties before assessing this option. Do not treat
    it as a route that lets day-1 migration proceed without the baseline gates.


    **Comparison** — The current direction (migrate into Mosaic''s own app) keeps
    control and one unified product but places the entire licensing question on Mosaic.
    The partner-bank option might transfer part of that burden but adds a dependency
    that cannot be stood up by Nov 15 and resolves none of the other four items. Where
    the state-by-state analysis shows Mosaic cannot be licensed in the Harbor-only
    states in time, this option — or the narrower launch already contemplated in the
    working approach — becomes the fallback worth pricing.

    ## Record conflicts


    1. **License counts do not support "four new markets."** Reported: Harbor 38,
    Mosaic 41, combined 44. Those numbers imply 35 shared states, 3 Harbor-only states,
    and 6 Mosaic-only states — not four new markets. Practical effect: the size of
    the licensing work before day 1 is unknown (3 states, 4 states, or a different
    set if some licenses are pending, conditional, or cover territories such as D.C.
    or Puerto Rico, which would also explain the discrepancy). Resolve with the state-by-state
    license schedules from both companies, including each license''s status.

    2. **Monitoring timing: "terminates at close" vs. "repoint on day 1."** The monitoring
    SaaS contract reportedly terminates at close; the repoint is planned for day 1.
    The records do not say whether those are the same moment or leave an unmonitored
    window. Practical effect: a possible coverage gap after close and unclear responsibility
    for alerts generated in it. Resolve with the vendor contract''s termination clause
    and the cutover schedule.

    3. **Reconciled, no open conflict:** the facts file still lists the deal structure
    as an unconfirmed assumption, while the later intake answer (asset purchase) is
    recorded as a fact. The later explicit report controls for this dossier; counsel
    may want the stale assumption retired so it does not re-enter the analysis.


    ## Assumptions used in this draft


    These are model assumptions, separate from the reported facts and from the assumptions
    recorded in the matter facts file. Ordered by effect.


    1. **Funds flow.** On day 1, migrated balances sit with Mosaic (not with Harbor
    or a bank), based on "one unified account, one balance" in Mosaic''s app. The
    licensing and account-transfer issues, and the assessment of the partner-bank
    alternative, depend on this; confirm with a funds-flow diagram.

    2. **Regulatory framework.** Mosaic Relay is a nonbank money transmitter subject
    to state MTL regimes and FinCEN/BSA requirements, not a prudentially regulated
    bank — so the bank CIP reliance rule is analogous rather than directly applicable.
    The KYC issue''s rule selection depends on this; confirm Mosaic''s regulatory
    status.

    3. **Meaning of "four new markets."** They are states where Harbor holds an MTL
    and Mosaic does not. The licensing issue''s scope depends on this; the record
    never defines the phrase, and the arithmetic is itself in conflict.

    4. **SAR handling.** Harbor''s SARs were filed with FinCEN, and the alert/SAR
    material can be reviewed through a confidentiality-respecting diligence channel.
    The alert/SAR handling plan depends on this.

    5. **Timing.** The Nov 15 close and day-1 migration remain fixed; the material
    read shows no change of date. All sequencing below assumes the remaining runway
    to Nov 15.


    ## Next actions


    **Common enabler:** the controlling documents — state license schedules, Mosaic''s
    AML/CIP policy, the monitoring vendor contract and cutover plan, the campaign
    terms, Harbor''s customer agreement, and the purchase agreement''s BSA/AML and
    data terms — were not retrieved for this dossier (the 24 captured documents were
    not read within the allowance). Each action depends on pulling its document.


    1. **Review the ~40 open alerts and the SAR history through a controlled channel.**
    Deliverable: privileged alert/SAR memo with account-level flags and any filing-gap
    assessment. Result needed to proceed: whether any migrated accounts carry unresolved
    suspicion or ongoing activity. Dependent decision: deal protections (specific
    indemnity, cooperation) and any account-level carve-outs from the day-1 book.
    Fallback if access is delayed: negotiate the indemnity and exclude unresolved
    accounts. **Proposed** owner: BSA/AML counsel with Harbor''s BSA officer and a
    clean team; start immediately — this feeds the close documents.

    2. **Confirm the KYC reliance basis.** Deliverable: compliance memo (policy text,
    applicability, cohort count). Result needed: whether reliance is permitted, and
    if not, the re-verification plan. Dependent decision: day-1 treatment of the pre-2023
    cohort (verify first, migrate with limits, or exclude). Fallback: step-up verification
    at or after migration with feature limits. **Proposed** owner: Mosaic compliance
    (the intake answer already directs this) with outside AML counsel; timing: early
    enough to feed the migration build.

    3. **State-by-state licensing analysis.** Deliverable: license matrix (status,
    activity coverage) and a day-1 go/no-go list, with applications or approvals started
    where needed. Result needed: which states Mosaic can serve on day 1. Dependent
    decisions: migration footprint and sequencing; the bonus campaign''s state list;
    and resolution of the license-count discrepancy. Fallback: two-wave launch, Harbor-only
    states excluded until cleared. **Proposed** owner: licensing/regulatory counsel;
    start immediately — state processing times are the constraint.

    4. **Monitoring cutover validation.** Deliverable: vendor contract review, cutover
    runbook, and test evidence. Result needed: a gap-free, tuned transition, or a
    decision to extend or parallel-run. Fallback: extend Harbor''s vendor contract
    or dual-run briefly. **Proposed** owner: Mosaic AML operations and engineering,
    with deal counsel on the contract; before close.

    5. **Welcome bonus terms and disclosures.** Deliverable: redlined terms and disclosures
    with a per-state availability list keyed to the licensing matrix. Result needed:
    a launchable campaign or a limited-state launch. Fallback: launch only in cleared
    states; defer the rest. **Proposed** owner: consumer-finance counsel with marketing;
    complete before close for a close+1 launch.

    6. **Privacy and account-transfer workstream.** Deliverable: data inventory, notice
    updates, and the migration notice/consent flow. Result needed: lawful basis and
    customer mechanics settled. Fallback: staged migration communications. **Proposed**
    owner: privacy counsel with product legal ops; before day 1.

    7. **Deal-document protections.** Deliverable: drafting instructions covering
    BSA/AML representations, a specific indemnity for pre-close alert/SAR exposure,
    filing and investigation cooperation, license transfer/cessation covenants, data
    terms, and — if the agreement remains open — a closing condition or interim operating
    covenant tied to the four gates. Result needed: confirm what the current agreement
    already allocates (not in the material read). Fallback: side letter or escrow
    if reopening the agreement is not feasible. **Proposed** owner: deal counsel;
    before close.


    **Timing note:** matter metadata records a target date of 2026-09-11 with no description;
    the only source-based deadlines in the record are the Nov 15 close and close+1
    for the campaign. The window for licensing and alert work is the binding constraint.

  - source_id: MSG-20260909-982278
    source_label: 'Saved message: From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

      Subject: Harbor migration — anything here …'
    source_class: saved_artifact
    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/conversations/CONV-20260909-a8160f.md
    available_excerpt: 'From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

      Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


      We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
      plan:


      240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1 post-close.
      One unified account, one balance, full access to our product set.

      No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

      Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice win,
      opens four new markets.

      Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
      results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
      2023.

      Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at close.
      Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day 1.

      Marketing wants a "Welcome" campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer, launching
      close+1.

      Diligence flagged that Harbor has ~40 open alerts and "a handful" of SARs from
      the last year. Nobody''s read them yet.


      Does any of this need legal before close? It''s really just a data migration.'
    record_revision: e847a82b62c8e0424b39f18d69bdf4564f21aad6b08303affc8f87a05f8782d1
    source_version: e847a82b62c8e0424b39f18d69bdf4564f21aad6b08303affc8f87a05f8782d1
    support_state: supplied

  - source_id: MSG-20260909-6caeae
    source_label: 'Saved message: Now let me give the lawyer the useful first answer.

      **Short answer: Yes — this i…'
    source_class: saved_artifact
    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/conversations/CONV-20260909-a8160f.md
    available_excerpt: 'Now let me give the lawyer the useful first answer.

      **Short answer: Yes — this is not "just a data migration."** Several items carry
      real regulatory and legal exposure that should be triaged before the Nov 15
      close. I''d rank them by risk:

      **1. The unread open alerts and SARs (highest risk).** ~40 open alerts and "a
      handful" of SARs from the last year that nobody has read is the single most
      decision-changing item. If any of those SARs reflect unresolved suspicious activity,
      you''re inheriting BSA/AML exposure at close. This needs review before close,
      not after — it can affect the deal itself, not just the migration. This is the
      first thing I''d want answered.

      **2. KYC records gap.** You have pass/fail results for everyone but not the
      underlying documents for pre-2023 users. Under BSA/AML customer identification
      and recordkeeping rules, relying on a prior acquirer''s KYC without the underlying
      documents is a real question — whether it''s a compliance gap depends on how
      you plan to satisfy your own CIP/recordkeeping obligations for those users.
      "No re-verification" may not be a safe default for the pre-2023 cohort.

      **3. Money transmission licensing for the four new markets.** The combined footprint
      "opens four new markets" — but that only works if Harbor''s MTLs transfer to
      Mosaic at close without new state approval. State MTL transfer/approval requirements
      vary, and this is a gating question for whether you can actually serve those
      markets on day 1.

      **4. Monitoring repoint.** Repointing Harbor''s transaction feed at your engine
      on day 1, with the SaaS contract terminating at close, creates a monitoring-continuity
      risk. If the repoint isn''t validated before close, you could have a gap in
      suspicious-activity monitoring.

      **5. The $50 welcome bonus.** Depending on structure (cash incentive vs. referral
      vs. promotional credit), this can trigger consumer disclosure, funds-flow, or
      state promotional requirements. Lower risk, but needs a quick check.

      **6. Data migration/privacy.** Moving 252k customers'' personal data is a data-protection
      and privacy matter, plus consumer funds-flow disclosures for migrated accounts.

      I''ve recorded the reported facts and flagged these as issues. To prioritize
      the work, the most decision-changing questions are:

      1. **Have the ~40 open alerts and SARs been reviewed, and what did they reveal?**
      (highest risk — could affect the deal)

      2. **For pre-2023 users with no underlying KYC documents, what''s the plan to
      satisfy Mosaic''s own BSA/AML obligations?**

      3. **For the four new markets, do Harbor''s MTLs transfer at close or is new
      state approval needed?**

      4. **How is the $50 welcome bonus structured?**

      The first one is the one I''d most want answered — it''s the item that could
      change the deal itself rather than just the migration plan.'

      require re-verification or access limits.

      - The bonus structure remains unknown.

    source_class: saved_artifact
    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/conversations/CONV-20260909-5299cf.md
    available_excerpt: '**Issue** — The four workstreams are licensing, KYC/AML, alerts
      and monitoring, and marketing.


      **Rule** — State licensing rules, Mosaic’s AML program, federal financial-crime
      duties, and consumer-protection rules may apply. **No external authority retrieved.**


      **Analysis**


      - **Licensing:** Asset purchases usually require state review of license transfer,
      assignment, or new applications. The four new markets may not be available at
      close.

      - **KYC/AML:** Mosaic must confirm whether its program permits reliance on Harbor’s
      checks. Missing records may require new verification or account limits.

      - **Alerts and monitoring:** Unresolved alerts need review. The monitoring transfer
      needs testing, audit records, and a plan that prevents coverage gaps.

      - **Marketing:** The $50 bonus needs clear eligibility, payment, expiry, tax,
      and advertising terms. State promotion rules may also apply.


      **Conclusion** — All four need legal or compliance review before launch. Licensing
      and unread alerts are the likely closing risks.'

      controls transfers, owes balances, or acts directly for users. KYC, alert, SAR,
      monitoring, and marketing questions remain.


      **Conclusion** — Map the funds flow, customer relationship, and compliance duties
      before assessing this option. The current matter position stays unchanged.

      content: '**Issue** — A partner bank could hold customer funds, while Mosaic
        supplies technology and operations.


        **Analysis** — This could lower licensing risk if the bank owns the accounts
        and controls fund transfers. It does not automatically remove risk if Mosaic
        controls transfers, owes balances, or acts directly for users. KYC, alert,
        SAR, monitoring, and marketing questions remain.


        **Conclusion** — Map the funds flow, customer relationship, and compliance
        duties before assessing this option. The current matter position stays unchanged.


        **No external authority retrieved for this hypothetical.**'

              path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-LOCAL-27b344a827f0cf86ced5.md
              revision: bfa5205c5c55347ff2e44736fdf58a3f8fade088059bc29b892ac7fa1e500afb

              passages: &id001
              - start: 0
                end: 817
                text: '# Issues and workstreams


                  - Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate
                  under the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor''s MTLs
                  transfer/survive the acquisition

                  - BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor''s prior KYC (with
                  missing underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic
                  Relay''s independent CIP/AML obligations

                  - SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage
                  Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability

                  - Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring
                  when the SaaS contract terminates at close

                  - Marketing compliance: the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state
                  money transmission or consumer protection implications

                  - Customer account, contract, and data-transfer rights <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-af341445a7af4c06
                  -->

                  '
              source_version: bfa5205c5c55347ff2e44736fdf58a3f8fade088059bc29b892ac7fa1e500afb
            source:SRC-LOCAL-5b01121f7bfd7357746c:
              kind: source
              record_id: SRC-LOCAL-5b01121f7bfd7357746c
              path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-LOCAL-5b01121f7bfd7357746c.md
              revision: 58b0379461c2b3d9c58807fff3ac3f7136d5aedd4f20022fc8be9eeb64cec409
              file_revision: 58b0379461c2b3d9c58807fff3ac3f7136d5aedd4f20022fc8be9eeb64cec409
              source_class: supplied_source
              availability: selected_passage
              reported: false
              passages: &id002
              - start: 0
                end: 3962
                text: '# Known Facts


                  - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10
                  weeks out).

                  - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                  into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account
                  and balance and full access to Mosaic''s product set.

                  - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d by
                  Harbor.

                  - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic
                  Relay holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new
                  markets.

                  - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic
                  has pass/fail results for everyone but not the underlying documents
                  for users onboarded before 2023.

                  - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
                  terminates at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction feed
                  at Mosaic''s engine on day 1.

                  - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on first
                  transfer, launching close+1.

                  - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from
                  the last year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

                  - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                  into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account
                  and balance.

                  - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users
                  were already KYC''d.

                  - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail
                  results exist for everyone but underlying documents are missing
                  for users onboarded before 2023.

                  - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
                  terminates at close; plan is to repoint the transaction feed to
                  Mosaic Relay''s engine on day 1.

                  - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from
                  the last year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

                  - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase
                  (Mosaic buys Harbor''s assets)

                  - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying
                  on another institution''s prior KYC without re-verification, or
                  is re-verification required? — Not sure / need to check with compliance

                  - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from
                  the last year? — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

                  - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does
                  Mosaic Relay plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or
                  apply for its own? — Use/assume Harbor''s licenses

                  - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents,
                  what is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer
                  identification and recordkeeping obligations? — It is not yet known
                  whether Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program permits reliance on Harbor''s
                  prior KYC; compliance must confirm.

                  - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last
                  year been reviewed, and what did they reveal? — The open alerts
                  and SAR history have not been reviewed and remain in diligence.

                  - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint,
                  what is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval
                  before onboarding those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans
                  to use or assume Harbor''s licenses for the four new markets.


                  ## Assumptions


                  - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses
                  and Harbor''s MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through
                  the acquisition without new state approval

                  - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy
                  Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying
                  documents

                  - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed
                  and validated before close without a monitoring gap

                  - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject
                  to state MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

                  - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter
                  in 41 states (per the request).

                  - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock
                  purchase, which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert
                  obligations transfer (structure not yet confirmed).

                  '
              source_version: 58b0379461c2b3d9c58807fff3ac3f7136d5aedd4f20022fc8be9eeb64cec409

                body_hash: 512d4a7a3e1afc61a66c79b53548e6795e9f434d557b21d346fd4662aaafc705
                path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000027.md
                text: "27 \n \n(c) \nThe audited financial statements shall include
                  or be accompanied by a \ncertificate of opinion of the independent
                  certified public accountant or independent public \naccountant that
                  is satisfactory in form and content to the [Commissioner]. If the
                  certificate or \nopinion is qualified, the [Commissioner] may order
                  the licensee to take any action as the \n[Commissioner] may find
                  necessary to enable the independent or certified public accountant
                  or \nindependent public accountant to remove the qualification.
                  \nSection 7.03 Authorized Delegate Reporting. \n(a) \nEach licensee
                  shall submit a report of authorized delegates within 45 days \nof
                  the end of the calendar quarter.20 The [Commissioner] is authorized
                  and encouraged to utilize \nNMLS for the submission of the report
                  required by this [Section 7.03(a)] provided that such \nfunctionality
                  is consistent with the requirements of this [Section 7.03]. \n(b)
                  \nThe authorized delegate report shall include, at a minimum, each
                  authorized \ndelegate's: \n(1) \nCompany legal name; \n(2) \nTaxpayer
                  employer identification number; \n(3) \nPrincipal provider identifier;
                  \n(4) \nPhysical address; \n(5) \nMailing address; \n(6) \nAny business
                  conducted in other states; \n(7) \nAny fictitious or trade name;
                  \n(8) \nContact person name, phone number, and email \n(9) \nStart
                  date as licensee’s authorized delegate; \n(10) \nEnd date acting
                  as licensee’s authorized delegate, if applicable;  \n(11) \n[Court
                  orders pursuant to [Section 8.03];] and \n(12) \nAny other information
                  the [Commissioner] reasonably requires with \nrespect to the authorized
                  delegate. \nSection 7.04 Reports of Certain Events.21 \n \n20 Commentary:
                  This language is designed to implement state use of the NMLS Uniform
                  Authorized Agent Reporting \n(UAAR) process. \n21 Commentary: States
                  are encouraged to utilize NMLS to satisfy Section 7.04 reporting
                  requirements if NMLS \ndevelops new functionality to prioritize
                  reporting of significant events.\n"
              - &id005
                unit_id: p000028
                start: 0
                end: 2132
                page_number: 28
                section_label: null
                body_hash: 80c098d06593529d6d6335e3b8a4fe8e8db356a8c5d82eb34a2001d27d642973
                path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000028.md
                text: "28 \n \n(a) \nA licensee shall file a report with the [Commissioner]
                  within one business \nday after the licensee has reason to know
                  of the occurrence of any of the following events: \n(1) \nthe filing
                  of a petition by or against the licensee under the \nUnited States
                  Bankruptcy Code, 11 U.S.C. Section 101-110, as amended or recodified
                  from \ntime to time, for bankruptcy or reorganization; \n(2) \nthe
                  filing of a petition by or against the licensee for \nreceivership,
                  the commencement of any other judicial or administrative proceeding

          title: issues.md
          support_state: supplied
          source_type: workspace
          available_excerpt: '# Issues and workstreams


            - Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under
            the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor''s MTLs transfer/survive
            the acquisition

            - BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor''s prior KYC (with missing
            underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay''s independent
            CIP/AML obligations

            - SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage Harbor''s
            ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability

            - Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring when
            the SaaS contract terminates at close

            - Marketing compliance: the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state money
            transmission or consumer protection implications

            - Customer account, contract, and data-transfer rights <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-af341445a7af4c06
            -->

            '

        - source_id: SRC-LOCAL-5b01121f7bfd7357746c
          source_hash: 58b0379461c2b3d9c58807fff3ac3f7136d5aedd4f20022fc8be9eeb64cec409

          path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-LOCAL-5b01121f7bfd7357746c.md
          original_path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md
          title: facts.md
          support_state: supplied
          source_type: workspace
          available_excerpt: '# Known Facts


            - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks
            out).

            - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic
            Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance
            and full access to Mosaic''s product set.

            - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d by Harbor.

            - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic
            Relay holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new markets.

            - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic has
            pass/fail results for everyone but not the underlying documents for users
            onboarded before 2023.

            - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
            terminates at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction feed at
            Mosaic''s engine on day 1.

            - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer,
            launching close+1.

            - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the
            last year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

            - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic
            Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance.

            - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users were
            already KYC''d.

            - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail
            results exist for everyone but underlying documents are missing for users
            onboarded before 2023.

            - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
            terminates at close; plan is to repoint the transaction feed to Mosaic
            Relay''s engine on day 1.

            - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the
            last year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

            - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase (Mosaic
            buys Harbor''s assets)

            - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying on another
            institution''s prior KYC without re-verification, or is re-verification
            required? — Not sure / need to check with compliance

            - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from the
            last year? — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

            - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does Mosaic
            Relay plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or apply for its
            own? — Use/assume Harbor''s licenses

            - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents, what
            is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer identification
            and recordkeeping obligations? — It is not yet known whether Mosaic Relay''s
            AML/CIP program permits reliance on Harbor''s prior KYC; compliance must
            confirm.

            - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last year
            been reviewed, and what did they reveal? — The open alerts and SAR history
            have not been reviewed and remain in diligence.

            - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint, what
            is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval before
            onboarding those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans to use or assume
            Harbor''s licenses for the four new markets.


            ## Assumptions


            - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses and
            Harbor''s MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through the acquisition
            without new state approval

            - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy Mosaic
            Relay''s own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying documents

            - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed and
            validated before close without a monitoring gap

            - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject to state
            MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

            - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter in
            41 states (per the request).

            - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock purchase,
            which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert obligations transfer
            (structure not yet confirmed).

            '
