            \n[Section 5.01(a)] does not apply to: \n(1) \nA person that is an authorized
            delegate of a person licensed under \nthis [Act] acting within the scope
            of authority conferred by a written contract with the \nlicensee; or \n(2)
            \nA person that is exempt pursuant to [Section 3.01] and does not \nengage
            in money transmission outside the scope of such exemption. \n(c) \nA license
            issued under [Section 5.05] is not transferable or assignable. \nSection
            5.02 Consistent State Licensing. \n(a) \nTo establish consistent licensing
            between [this state] and other states, the \n[Commissioner] is authorized
            and encouraged to: \n(1) \nimplement all licensing provisions of this
            [Act] in a manner that is \nconsistent with other states that have adopted
            this [Act]or multistate licensing processes; \nand \n(2) \nparticipate
            in nationwide protocols for licensing cooperation and \ncoordination among
            state regulators provided that such protocols are consistent with this
            \n[Act]. \n(b) \nIn order to fulfill the purposes of this [Act], the [Commissioner]
            is \nauthorized and encouraged to establish relationships or contracts
            with NMLS or other entities \ndesignated by NMLS to enable the [Commissioner]
            to: \n(1) \ncollect and maintain records; \n(2) \ncoordinate multistate
            licensing processes and supervision processes; \n(3) \nprocess fees; and
            \n(4) \nfacilitate communication between [state] and licensees or other
            \npersons subject to this [Act]. \n(c) \nThe [Commissioner] is authorized
            and encouraged to utilize NMLS for all \naspects of licensing in accordance
            with this [Act], including but not limited to, license applications, \napplications
            for acquisitions of control, surety bonds, reporting, criminal history
            background\n"

          available_excerpt: "22 \n \n(e) \nWhen an application for acquisition of
            control under this [Section 6.01] \nappears to include all the items and
            address all of the matters that are required, the application shall \nbe
            considered complete and the [Commissioner] shall promptly notify the applicant
            in a record of \nthe date on which the application was determined to be
            complete and:15 \n \n(1) \nThe [Commissioner] shall approve or deny the
            application within 60 \ndays after the completion date; or \n(2) \nif
            the application is not approved or denied within 60 days after the \ncompletion
            date: \n(A) \nthe application is approved; and \n(B) \nthe person, or
            group of persons acting in concert, are not \nprohibited from acquiring
            control. \n(3) \nThe [Commissioner] may for good cause extend the application
            \nperiod. \n(f) \nA determination by the [Commissioner] that an application
            is complete and \nis accepted for processing means only that the application,
            on its face, appears to include all of the \nitems and address all of
            the matters that are required, and is not an assessment of the substance
            of \nthe application or of the sufficiency of the information provided.
            \n(g) \nWhen an application is filed and considered complete under [Section
            \n6.01(e)], the [Commissioner] shall investigate the financial condition
            and responsibility, financial \nand business experience, character, and
            general fitness of the person, or group of persons acting in \nconcert,
            seeking to acquire control. The [Commissioner] shall approve an acquisition
            of control \npursuant to this [Section 6.01] if the [Commissioner] finds
            that all of the following conditions have \nbeen fulfilled: \n(1) \nThe
            requirements of subsections (b) and (d) have been met, as \napplicable;
            and \n(2) \nthe financial condition and responsibility, financial and
            business \nexperience, competence, character, and general fitness of the
            person, or group of persons \nacting in concert, seeking to acquire control;
            and the competence, experience, character, \nand general fitness of the
            key individuals and persons that would be in control of the \nlicensee
            after the acquisition of control indicate that it is in the interest of
            the public to \npermit the person, or group of persons acting in concert,
            to control the licensee. \n(h) \nIf an applicant avails itself or is otherwise
            subject to a multistate licensing \n \n15 Commentary: NMLS will accommodate
            and streamline the process of communicating when applications are \nreceived
            and when states consider them to have been complete. The intent of this
            Act is for the application period to \nbegin on the day an application
            is determined to be complete.\n"

          available_excerpt: "23 \n \nprocess: \n(1) \nthe [Commissioner] is authorized

            state for the purpose of [Section 6.01(g)] if the \nlead investigative

            \nif [state] is a lead investigative state, the [Commissioner] is \nauthorized

            set forth in the notice of denial the specific reasons for the denial

            [Commissioner] under this [Section \n6.01(i)] may appeal within thirty
            (30) days16 after receipt of the written notice of the denial \n[pursuant
            to state administrative law procedures]. \n(j) \nThe requirements of [Section
            6.01(a) and (b)] do not apply to any of the \nfollowing: \n(1) \nA person
            that acts as a proxy for the sole purpose of voting at a \ndesignated
            meeting of the shareholders or holders of voting shares or voting interests
            of a \nlicensee or a person in control of a licensee; \n(2) \nA person
            that acquires control of a licensee by devise or descent; \n(3) \nA person
            that acquires control of a licensee as a personal \nrepresentative, custodian,
            guardian, conservator, or trustee, or as an officer appointed by a \ncourt
            of competent jurisdiction or by operation of law; \n(4) \nA person that
            is exempt under [Section 3.01(g)]; \n(5) \nA person that the [Commissioner]
            determines is not subject to \n[Section 6.01(a)] based on the public interest;
            \n(6) \nA public offering of securities of a licensee or a person in control
            of \na licensee; or \n(7) \nAn internal reorganization of a person in

            (4), (6), (7)] in cooperation with the \nlicensee shall notify the [Commissioner]
            within [15] days after the acquisition of control.17 \n \n16 Commentary:
            Administrative procedures for challenging a departmental decision may

            Commentary: Notice is satisfied upon updating the licensee’s NMLS record.\n"

            holds money in trust for the benefit of a \nlicensee and knowingly fails
            to remit more than [$XXX] of such money is guilty of a [reference \nto

          unit_id: s000001
          locator: Section 1, characters 2400–7324
          available_excerpt: 'ey Transmitter License.


            Access to NMLS


            NMLS is a secure web-based system created by state regulators to provide
            efficiencies in the processing of state licenses and improve supervision
            of state-regulated industries.


            To access NMLS for the first time, you must complete a Company Account
            Request Form and identify a Primary Account Administrator and a Secondary
            Account Administrator. This form can be submitted online through the NMLS
            website in the Getting Started section. This form needs to be submitted
            only once per company, regardless of the number of NMLS participating
            states in which you are licensed.


            Within three days of completing and submitting the Company Account Request
            Form, the Primary Account Administrator will receive NMLS login information.
            The Primary Account Administrator will have full rights to access the
            system, submit information to this agency and other participating state
            regulators, and set up other company users in the system. Instructions
            and tutorials on how to access and use the system are also available in
            the NMLS Resource Center .


            Note : If your company already has a record in NMLS, you can omit this
            step.


            Managing Your License on NMLS


            Each company holding a DFS Money Transmitter License who wishes to manage
            their license on NMLS must create a company record in the system. To gain
            access to NMLS, the applicant must submit a form requesting an NMLS account.


            Current New York State Money Transmitters may transition their licenses
            to NMLS. See the DFS Money Transmitter Transition Checklist for more information.


            Submitting a Complete Application


            To submit an application and ensure your application is received, acknowledged
            as complete, and processed, please follow the instructions on the DFS
            Money Transmitter Checklists . No application shall be deemed to be complete
            until the Department has received all required information, documents,
            and fees.


            In the process of reviewing and considering the application, DFS may request
            additional information and supporting documents.


            In the application process, an NMLS Identification Number will be assigned
            to your application. Please maintain a record of this NMLS Identification
            Number, as it will be used as your application reference number throughout
            the remainder of the application process. The applicant’s NMLS Identification
            Number must be included on every hard-copy document submitted to the Department.


            Note : If the applicant has already submitted Forms MU1 and MU2 through
            NMLS for another state, the applicant does not need to re-enter the company
            record into NMLS. However, the applicant is required to provide jurisdiction-specific
            information to support its New York State application.


            Back to Top ▲


            Next Section


            Continue


            Annual Reporting


            The Annual Report should be prepared by qualified persons and submitted
            within 120 days following the close of the calendar year January 1 to
            December 31, 2025.


            2025 NMLS Money Transmitter Annual Report Form


            2025 Non-NMLS Money Transmitter Annual Report Form


            Back to Top ▲


            Next Section


            Continue


            Reporting Change in Certain Individuals


            Pursuant to the following sections of the New York Banking Law (BL) and
            Superintendent’s Regulations (SR), licensees of the Department of Financial
            Services (DFS) are required to notify the Superintendent of changes in
            certain individuals, within stipulated time frames:


            Money Transmitters: BL 641, 642 and 652-a; and SR 406.11


            These requirements are for changes in certain individuals of licensees
            whose licenses are not managed on NMLS. For those managed on NMLS, visit
            the NMLS section website for New York State and navigate to Company Licenses
            and Amendment under the pertinent industry type, and look under Change
            in Control on the Amendment Checklist.


            Included Individuals


            Members of the governing board such as directors, trustees, and LLC members


            Officers (at a minimum Chief Executive Officer, President, Chief Financial
            Officer, Chief Compliance Officer, and Chief Operations Officer, and any
            other officers deemed necessary by DFS)


            Documentary requirements for Each Included Individual Being Added


            Notification on the licensee''s letterhead signed by an authorized officer
            containing the following:


            Name and title of the individual being added


            Effective date of the addition


            Name and title of the person being replaced, and his/her new title/position,
            if any


            Resolution of the governing board approving the addition


            Personal Questionnaire (PDF)


            Fingerprints


            Background Investigation Report *


            Litigation Affidavit (PDF)


            Authority to Release Information (PDF)


            Resume


            Documentary requirements for Each Included Individual Being Removed:


            Notification on the licensee''s letterhead signed by an authorized officer
            containing the following:


            Name and title of the individual being removed


            Reason of the removal


            Effective date of the removal


            New title/position, if any


            Where To Submit?'

          source_hash: b8cfb71cc698f4b53cce08d023441fce54bf275adbcb1164dfb05a05143f6ba9
          source_label: How To Get A Money Transmitter License (MTL) in the U.S. -
            Fenergo — Section 2, characters 0–3321
          unit_id: s000002
          locator: Section 2, characters 0–3321
          available_excerpt: 'How To Get A Money Transmitter License (MTL) in the
            U.S.


            Published Date  January 29, 2026


            To get a Money Transmitter License (MTL), businesses must undergo a rigorous
            application process that involves dual compliance with federal (like FinCEN''s
            AML/KYC protocols) and varying state-level regulations. Key requirements
            across states include demonstrating financial viability, often requiring
            a surety bond and capital reserves, passing comprehensive background checks
            for key personnel, and establishing a robust internal compliance program.
            The process is complex, time-consuming, and mandates extensive documentation
            and financial disclosures to ensure the applicant is law-abiding and financially
            sound.


            Operating a money transfer service in the U.S. involves tackling a myriad
            of federal and state laws, making how to get a money transmitter license
            both time-consuming and expensive. Compliance with agencies like FinCEN
            is non-negotiable to prevent illegal activities.


            Companies can either secure their own MSB license or partner with a licensed
            entity, but legal adherence is vital in both scenarios. It''s essential
            to understand what a money transmitter license is and who needs it.


            What is a Money Transmitter License?


            A Money Transmitter License is an official authorization or money service
            business license that empowers a firm or individual to facilitate the
            movement of capital. This license enables MSBs to handle financial transactions,
            ranging from digital payments to wire transfers.


            Possessing a Money Transmitter License brings forth substantial regulatory
            oversight. Organizations must prove they have the governance structure
            and internal controls to manage and safeguard client funds. States will
            continually scrutinize applicants, denying licensure to those who fail
            to meet the stringent criteria.


            In the United States, the need for a Money Transmitter License is not
            a choice; it''s a requirement for virtually any business involved in the
            handling or transferring of funds. Money transmitter license requirements
            by state can vary, so it''s crucial to be aware of the respective state
            money transmitter regulations.


            How to Get a Money Transmitter License?


            The license application process is designed to be rigorous, ensuring that
            approved businesses are law-abiding and financially sound. Federal and
            state-level regulations diverge, with each state setting its own financial
            criteria and often requiring a minimum capital commitment.


            Applicants typically need a surety bond of at least $500,000 per state,
            with costs influenced by credit history. The duration to obtain the license
            varies, contingent on the business type and the state of operation.


            Money Transmitter License Requirements


            Acquiring a money transmitter license involves compliance with Anti-Money
            Laundering (AML) and Know Your Customer (KYC) protocols. While these regulations
            are federal, individual states often impose additional requirements, thereby
            necessitating dual compliance.


            Subsequent to application submission, state authorities undertake an investigative
            review, focusing on financial sustainability and the applicant''s background.


            Standardized Requirements Across States


            Registration: Initial registration typically occurs with the Financial
            Crimes Enforcement Network or a similar state-level body.'

          source_label: OCC Confirms National Bank Act Preempts State Money Transmitter
            ... — Section 1, characters 600–4794
          unit_id: s000001
          locator: Section 1, characters 600–4794
          available_excerpt: ', 2026


            Posted in Bank Regulatory


            On May 12, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued
            a significant interpretive letter confirming that Fidelity Digital Assets,
            National Association (the recently converted national trust bank formerly
            known as Fidelity Digital Assets Service, LLC) is not required to hold
            state money transmitter licenses to conduct its federally authorized activities.
            The OCC concluded that the National Bank Act preempts any state money
            transmitter licensing requirement as applied to a national bank.


            Until December 12, 2025, Fidelity Digital Assets operated as a New York-chartered
            limited liability trust company and held money transmitter licenses in
            numerous states, including Iowa. On that date, the OCC approved its conversion
            to an uninsured national trust bank under 12 U.S.C. § 27(a). Concurrent
            with the conversion, the Bank surrendered its Iowa money transmitter license.


            Iowa pushed back. Its money transmitter statute exempts banks and trust
            companies from licensing, but only if they hold federally insured deposits.
            Because Fidelity Digital Assets is an uninsured national bank, Iowa argued
            the exemption did not apply and requested a legal basis for the license
            surrender. Fidelity Digital Assets responded that the National Bank Act
            preempts Iowa’s requirements and asked the OCC to confirm that position.


            The OCC’s analysis of whether a state can require a national bank to obtain
            a state money transmitter license as a condition of engaging in federally
            authorized activities, including cryptocurrency custody, trade execution,
            stablecoin issuance, and related digital asset services, rested on two
            independent and well-established pillars of federal banking law:


            1. National Bank Act Preemption


            Federal law authorizes national banks to conduct a broad range of activities
            on a national basis. Any state law that “prevents or significantly interferes”
            with a national bank’s exercise of its federally authorized powers is
            preempted.


            The OCC reasoned that requiring a national bank to obtain a state money
            transmitter license, even as a threshold condition to operating, would
            impermissibly condition the Bank’s federal authority on state approval.
            At the extreme, a state could veto federal authority outright by denying
            or revoking a license. Both outcomes are squarely preempted. This conclusion
            applies to any state’s money transmitter licensing regime, including states
            that limit their licensing exemptions to a subset of national banks (such
            as Iowa’s insured-deposits-only carveout).


            2. Exclusive Federal Visitorial Authority


            Separately, 12 U.S.C. § 484 vests the OCC with exclusive visitorial authority
            over national banks. “No national bank shall be subject to any visitorial
            powers except as authorized by Federal law.” Iowa’s money transmitter
            statute grants the state agency robust supervisory jurisdiction over licensees,
            including the power to demand books and records, conduct periodic examinations,
            take enforcement actions, and even place a licensee into receivership.
            Applying that regime to a national bank would be “fundamentally inconsistent”
            with the OCC’s exclusive visitorial powers and is therefore impermissible
            on independent grounds.


            Together, these two bases lead to a clean and sweeping conclusion: a national
            bank may conduct its federally authorized activities in any state without
            a state money transmitter license, regardless of whether it qualifies
            for any state-law exemption.


            Our Take


            The OCC’s conclusion here was entirely expected. The preemption framework
            for national banks is well-settled, and the OCC’s letter largely restates
            principles the Supreme Court and federal courts have applied for decades.
            That said, one nuance in this letter deserves closer attention: state-chartered
            trust banks are in a very different position.


            Unlike national banks, state trust companies and state-chartered banks
            do not benefit from National Bank Act preemption. Their ability to avoid
            state money transmitter licensing requirements depends entirely on how
            each individual state defines “bank” or “trust company” in its money transmission
            statute and those definitions vary considerably.

              path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-LOCAL-db6468aeb552bb44aa7b.md

              passages: &id025
              - start: 0
                end: 1441
                text: '# Issues and workstreams


                  - Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate
                  under the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor''s MTLs
                  transfer/survive the acquisition

                  - BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor''s prior KYC (with
                  missing underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic
                  Relay''s independent CIP/AML obligations

                  - SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage
                  Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability

                  - Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring
                  when the SaaS contract terminates at close

                  - Marketing compliance: the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state
                  money transmission or consumer protection implications

                  - Customer account, contract, and data-transfer rights <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-af341445a7af4c06
                  -->

                  - Open alerts, suspicious activity history, and acquisition diligence
                  <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-d22ea3957f21252a -->

                  - State money-transmission authority after the asset purchase <!--
                  issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-65ae94508dcda1bf -->

                  - Reliance on Harbor’s prior identity verification <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-30caa16a9234ccf2
                  -->

                  - Transaction-monitoring continuity at cutover <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-1d13a6636b8fbe60
                  -->

                  - Purchase-agreement authority and risk allocation <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-29efc151650e76a2
                  -->

                  - Customer terms, privacy, data transfers, and welcome bonus <!--
                  issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-fcd3954739e05481 -->

                  '
              source_version: 916b7009f261c21b7029be2ac4bab07fb4fd2909920244882bc8c02250c75dac

              path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-LOCAL-5b01121f7bfd7357746c.md
              revision: 58b0379461c2b3d9c58807fff3ac3f7136d5aedd4f20022fc8be9eeb64cec409

              passages: &id026
              - start: 0
                end: 3962
                text: '# Known Facts


                  - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10
                  weeks out).

                  - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                  into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account
                  and balance and full access to Mosaic''s product set.

                  - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d by
                  Harbor.

                  - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic
                  Relay holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new
                  markets.

                  - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic
                  has pass/fail results for everyone but not the underlying documents
                  for users onboarded before 2023.

                  - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
                  terminates at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction feed
                  at Mosaic''s engine on day 1.

                  - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on first
                  transfer, launching close+1.

                  - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from
                  the last year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

                  - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                  into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account
                  and balance.

                  - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users
                  were already KYC''d.

                  - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail
                  results exist for everyone but underlying documents are missing
                  for users onboarded before 2023.

                  - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
                  terminates at close; plan is to repoint the transaction feed to
                  Mosaic Relay''s engine on day 1.

                  - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from
                  the last year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

                  - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase
                  (Mosaic buys Harbor''s assets)

                  - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying
                  on another institution''s prior KYC without re-verification, or
                  is re-verification required? — Not sure / need to check with compliance

                  - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from
                  the last year? — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

                  - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does
                  Mosaic Relay plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or
                  apply for its own? — Use/assume Harbor''s licenses

                  - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents,
                  what is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer
                  identification and recordkeeping obligations? — It is not yet known
                  whether Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program permits reliance on Harbor''s
                  prior KYC; compliance must confirm.

                  - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last
                  year been reviewed, and what did they reveal? — The open alerts
                  and SAR history have not been reviewed and remain in diligence.

                  - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint,
                  what is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval
                  before onboarding those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans
                  to use or assume Harbor''s licenses for the four new markets.


                  ## Assumptions


                  - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses
                  and Harbor''s MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through
                  the acquisition without new state approval

                  - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy
                  Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying
                  documents

                  - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed
                  and validated before close without a monitoring gap

                  - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject
                  to state MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

                  - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter
                  in 41 states (per the request).

                  - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock
                  purchase, which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert
                  obligations transfer (structure not yet confirmed).

                  '
              source_version: 58b0379461c2b3d9c58807fff3ac3f7136d5aedd4f20022fc8be9eeb64cec409

          available_excerpt: '# Issues and workstreams


            - Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under
            the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor''s MTLs transfer/survive
            the acquisition

            - BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor''s prior KYC (with missing
            underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay''s independent
            CIP/AML obligations

            - SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage Harbor''s
            ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability

            - Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring when
            the SaaS contract terminates at close

            - Marketing compliance: the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state money
            transmission or consumer protection implications

            - Customer account, contract, and data-transfer rights <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-af341445a7af4c06
            -->

            - Open alerts, suspicious activity history, and acquisition diligence
            <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-d22ea3957f21252a -->

            - State money-transmission authority after the asset purchase <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-65ae94508dcda1bf
            -->

            - Reliance on Harbor’s prior identity verification <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-30caa16a9234ccf2
            -->

            - Transaction-monitoring continuity at cutover <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-1d13a6636b8fbe60
            -->

            - Purchase-agreement authority and risk allocation <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-29efc151650e76a2
            -->

            - Customer terms, privacy, data transfers, and welcome bonus <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-fcd3954739e05481
            -->

            '

          path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-LOCAL-5b01121f7bfd7357746c.md
          original_path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md
          title: facts.md
          support_state: supplied
          source_type: workspace
          available_excerpt: '# Known Facts


            - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks
            out).

            - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic
            Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance
            and full access to Mosaic''s product set.

            - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d by Harbor.

            - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic
            Relay holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new markets.

            - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic has
            pass/fail results for everyone but not the underlying documents for users
            onboarded before 2023.

            - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
            terminates at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction feed at
            Mosaic''s engine on day 1.

            - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer,
            launching close+1.

            - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the
            last year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

            - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic
            Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance.

            - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users were
            already KYC''d.

            - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail
            results exist for everyone but underlying documents are missing for users
            onboarded before 2023.

            - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
            terminates at close; plan is to repoint the transaction feed to Mosaic
            Relay''s engine on day 1.

            - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the
            last year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

            - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase (Mosaic
            buys Harbor''s assets)

            - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying on another
            institution''s prior KYC without re-verification, or is re-verification
            required? — Not sure / need to check with compliance

            - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from the
            last year? — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

            - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does Mosaic
            Relay plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or apply for its
            own? — Use/assume Harbor''s licenses

            - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents, what
            is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer identification
            and recordkeeping obligations? — It is not yet known whether Mosaic Relay''s
            AML/CIP program permits reliance on Harbor''s prior KYC; compliance must
            confirm.

            - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last year
            been reviewed, and what did they reveal? — The open alerts and SAR history
            have not been reviewed and remain in diligence.

            - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint, what
            is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval before
            onboarding those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans to use or assume
            Harbor''s licenses for the four new markets.


            ## Assumptions


            - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses and
            Harbor''s MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through the acquisition
            without new state approval

            - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy Mosaic
            Relay''s own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying documents

            - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed and
            validated before close without a monitoring gap

            - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject to state
            MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

            - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter in
            41 states (per the request).

            - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock purchase,
            which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert obligations transfer
            (structure not yet confirmed).

            '

            - question_id: Q-SAR
              text: Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last
                year been reviewed, and what did they reveal?
              consequence: Unread open alerts and SARs are the highest-risk item;
                they can create BSA/AML exposure that must be addressed before close
                and could affect the deal itself.
              state: answered
              answer: The open alerts and SAR history have not been reviewed and remain
                in diligence.
              answer_kind: reported_fact
              linked_fact_ids:
              - FACT-20260909-070aec
            - question_id: Q-KYC
              text: For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents,
                what is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay's own BSA/AML customer identification
                and recordkeeping obligations?
              consequence: Whether the missing underlying documents create a compliance
                gap depends on how Mosaic plans to satisfy its own CIP/recordkeeping
                obligations for these users.
              state: answered
              answer: It is not yet known whether Mosaic Relay's AML/CIP program permits
                reliance on Harbor's prior KYC; compliance must confirm.
              answer_kind: reported_fact
              linked_fact_ids:
              - FACT-20260909-620c62
            - question_id: Q-MTL
              text: For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint,
                what is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval
                before onboarding those customers?
              consequence: Whether the four new markets can be served at close depends
                on license transferability and state approval, which is a gating regulatory
                question.
              state: answered
              answer: Mosaic Relay currently plans to use or assume Harbor's licenses
                for the four new markets.
              answer_kind: reported_fact
              linked_fact_ids:
              - FACT-20260909-771ee1
            - question_id: Q-BONUS
              text: How is the $50 welcome bonus structured?
              consequence: The structure determines whether the bonus triggers consumer
                disclosure, funds-flow, or state promotional requirements.

      privacy, data transfers, and welcome bonus. Migration could change the service
      provider, account access, available products, data recipients, and customer
      rights. The proposed $50 bonus adds advertising and offer-term risk.\nLawyer's
      accepted priorities (private matter context):\nPrevent a monitoring gap and
      keep a staged-launch option available.: A failed cutover can create immediate
      compliance and customer harm. A controlled delay preserves reversibility.\nProposed
      date leads; resolve each reference in saved records before using it: [{\"role\":
      \"target acquisition close\", \"value\": \"Nov 15\", \"source_reference_id\":
      \"MSG-20260909-982278\", \"note\": \"The source describes this date as about

      \"MSG-20260909-982278\", \"note\": \"The record reports that Harbor\\u2019s

              - start: 0
                end: 3962
                text: '# Known Facts


                  - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10
                  weeks out).

                  - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                  into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account
                  and balance and full access to Mosaic''s product set.

                  - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d by
                  Harbor.

                  - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic
                  Relay holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new
                  markets.

                  - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic
                  has pass/fail results for everyone but not the underlying documents
                  for users onboarded before 2023.

                  - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
                  terminates at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction feed
                  at Mosaic''s engine on day 1.

                  - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on first
                  transfer, launching close+1.

                  - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from
                  the last year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

                  - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                  into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account
                  and balance.

                  - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users
                  were already KYC''d.

                  - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail
                  results exist for everyone but underlying documents are missing
                  for users onboarded before 2023.

                  - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
                  terminates at close; plan is to repoint the transaction feed to
                  Mosaic Relay''s engine on day 1.

                  - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from
                  the last year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

                  - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase
                  (Mosaic buys Harbor''s assets)

                  - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying
                  on another institution''s prior KYC without re-verification, or
                  is re-verification required? — Not sure / need to check with compliance

                  - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from
                  the last year? — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

                  - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does
                  Mosaic Relay plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or
                  apply for its own? — Use/assume Harbor''s licenses

                  - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents,
                  what is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer
                  identification and recordkeeping obligations? — It is not yet known
                  whether Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program permits reliance on Harbor''s
                  prior KYC; compliance must confirm.

                  - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last
                  year been reviewed, and what did they reveal? — The open alerts
                  and SAR history have not been reviewed and remain in diligence.

                  - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint,
                  what is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval
                  before onboarding those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans
                  to use or assume Harbor''s licenses for the four new markets.


                  ## Assumptions


                  - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses
                  and Harbor''s MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through
                  the acquisition without new state approval

                  - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy
                  Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying
                  documents

                  - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed
                  and validated before close without a monitoring gap

                  - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject
                  to state MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

                  - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter
                  in 41 states (per the request).

                  - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock
                  purchase, which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert
                  obligations transfer (structure not yet confirmed).

                  '
              source_version: 58b0379461c2b3d9c58807fff3ac3f7136d5aedd4f20022fc8be9eeb64cec409

              - start: 0

                text: '# Issues and workstreams


                  - Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate
                  under the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor''s MTLs
                  transfer/survive the acquisition

                  - BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor''s prior KYC (with
                  missing underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic
                  Relay''s independent CIP/AML obligations

                  - SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage
                  Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability

                  - Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring
                  when the SaaS contract terminates at close

                  - Marketing compliance: the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state
                  money transmission or consumer protection implications

                  - Customer account, contract, and data-transfer rights <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-af341445a7af4c06
                  -->

                  - Open alerts, suspicious activity history, and acquisition diligence
                  <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-d22ea3957f21252a -->

                  - State money-transmission authority after the asset purchase <!--
                  issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-65ae94508dcda1bf -->

                  - Reliance on Harbor’s prior identity verification <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-30caa16a9234ccf2
                  -->

                  - Transaction-monitoring continuity at cutover <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-1d13a6636b8fbe60
                  -->

                  - Purchase-agreement authority and risk allocation <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-29efc151650e76a2
                  -->

                  - Customer terms, privacy, data transfers, and welcome bonus <!--
                  issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-fcd3954739e05481 -->

                  '

              passages: &id030
              - start: 0
                end: 2312
                text: '## Preparation note


                  **Result:** Legal and compliance review is required before the Nov
                  15 close. The migration is not only a technical data transfer.


                  **Lawyer reframe:** Determine which pre-close and day-one actions
                  could change the deal risk, exceed Mosaic’s legal authority, weaken
                  anti-money-laundering controls, or harm customers. Then separate
                  safe preparation from actions that require legal clearance.


                  The current plan relies on unconfirmed assumptions. Harbor’s licenses
                  might not transfer in an asset purchase. Mosaic might not be able
                  to rely on Harbor’s identity checks. About 40 alerts and several
                  suspicious activity reports remain unreviewed. Harbor’s monitoring
                  service will end at close, but the replacement has not been shown
                  to work.


                  The safer route is a staged launch. Mosaic can complete reversible
                  technical work before close. It should delay affected accounts,
                  new markets, or full product access if a legal or compliance gate
                  remains open.


                  ### Material issues


                  - Unresolved alerts and suspicious activity history.

                  - State money-transmission authority after the asset purchase.

                  - Reliance on identity checks that lack underlying records.

                  - Continuous transaction monitoring at cutover.

                  - Purchase-agreement limits and allocation of compliance liabilities.

                  - Customer terms, privacy notices, data transfers, and the $50 bonus.


                  ### Three business priorities


                  1. **Protect the acquisition decision.** Review unresolved compliance
                  matters before Mosaic accepts risk that is difficult to reverse.

                  2. **Confirm lawful day-one service.** Verify that Mosaic can serve
                  each account and market after an asset purchase.

                  3. **Preserve a safe fallback.** Keep monitoring active and permit
                  a staged launch if any required control is not ready.


                  ### First three issues to research


                  1. **Open alerts and suspicious activity history.** The findings
                  could change deal terms, closing conditions, remediation, or account
                  eligibility.

                  2. **State licensing.** Regulatory approval could take time and
                  could prevent launch in the four new markets.

                  3. **Identity-verification reliance.** Missing source records affect
                  240,000 consumers and 12,000 business accounts and could require
                  re-verification or access limits.




                  > A requested saved-record read was unavailable. The writer used
                  the material available.

                  '
              source_version: 23fcb27105945705c2b19c1547c310303a49b7d909b07a52e0fe3323e0ae2e9a

              - start: 0
                end: 1095
                text: '# Original Request


                  From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

                  Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


                  We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks).
                  Migration plan:


                  240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on
                  day 1 post-close. One unified account, one balance, full access
                  to our product set.

                  No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

                  Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44
                  — nice win, opens four new markets.

                  Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have
                  pass/fail results for everyone, but not the underlying documents
                  for users onboarded before 2023.

                  Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates
                  at close. Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine
                  on day 1.

                  Marketing wants a "Welcome" campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer,
                  launching close+1.

                  Diligence flagged that Harbor has ~40 open alerts and "a handful"
                  of SARs from the last year. Nobody''s read them yet.


                  Does any of this need legal before close? It''s really just a data
                  migration.

                  '

            AML/CIP program permits reliance on Harbor''s prior KYC; compliance must
            confirm.

            - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last year
            been reviewed, and what did they reveal? — The open alerts and SAR history
            have not been reviewed and remain in diligence.

            - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint, what
            is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval before
            onboarding those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans to use or assume
            Harbor''s licenses for the four new markets.


            ## Assumptions


            - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses and
            Harbor''s MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through the acquisition
            without new state approval

            - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy Mosaic
            Relay''s own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying documents

            - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed and
            validated before close without a monitoring gap

            - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject to state
            MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

            - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter in
            41 states (per the request).

            - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock purchase,
            which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert obligations transfer
            (structure not yet confirmed).

            '

          path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-LOCAL-8f6233be11b7205ffc25.md
          original_path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/dossier-requests/DOR-20260912-049f9c.md
          title: DOR-20260912-049f9c.md
          support_state: supplied
          source_type: workspace
          available_excerpt: '## Preparation note


            **Result:** Legal and compliance review is required before the Nov 15
            close. The migration is not only a technical data transfer.


            **Lawyer reframe:** Determine which pre-close and day-one actions could
            change the deal risk, exceed Mosaic’s legal authority, weaken anti-money-laundering
            controls, or harm customers. Then separate safe preparation from actions
            that require legal clearance.


            The current plan relies on unconfirmed assumptions. Harbor’s licenses
            might not transfer in an asset purchase. Mosaic might not be able to rely
            on Harbor’s identity checks. About 40 alerts and several suspicious activity
            reports remain unreviewed. Harbor’s monitoring service will end at close,
            but the replacement has not been shown to work.


            The safer route is a staged launch. Mosaic can complete reversible technical
            work before close. It should delay affected accounts, new markets, or
            full product access if a legal or compliance gate remains open.


            ### Material issues


            - Unresolved alerts and suspicious activity history.

            - State money-transmission authority after the asset purchase.

            - Reliance on identity checks that lack underlying records.

            - Continuous transaction monitoring at cutover.

            - Purchase-agreement limits and allocation of compliance liabilities.

            - Customer terms, privacy notices, data transfers, and the $50 bonus.


            ### Three business priorities


            1. **Protect the acquisition decision.** Review unresolved compliance
            matters before Mosaic accepts risk that is difficult to reverse.

            2. **Confirm lawful day-one service.** Verify that Mosaic can serve each
            account and market after an asset purchase.

            3. **Preserve a safe fallback.** Keep monitoring active and permit a staged
            launch if any required control is not ready.


            ### First three issues to research


            1. **Open alerts and suspicious activity history.** The findings could
            change deal terms, closing conditions, remediation, or account eligibility.

            2. **State licensing.** Regulatory approval could take time and could
            prevent launch in the four new markets.

            3. **Identity-verification reliance.** Missing source records affect 240,000
            consumers and 12,000 business accounts and could require re-verification
            or access limits.




            > A requested saved-record read was unavailable. The writer used the material
            available.

            '

          title: request.md
          support_state: supplied
          source_type: workspace
          available_excerpt: '# Original Request


            From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

            Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


            We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
            plan:


            240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1
            post-close. One unified account, one balance, full access to our product
            set.

            No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

            Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice
            win, opens four new markets.

            Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
            results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded
            before 2023.

            Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at
            close. Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day
            1.

            Marketing wants a "Welcome" campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer,
            launching close+1.

            Diligence flagged that Harbor has ~40 open alerts and "a handful" of SARs
            from the last year. Nobody''s read them yet.


            Does any of this need legal before close? It''s really just a data migration.

            '

              title: Transaction-monitoring continuity at cutover
              why_it_matters: Harbor’s monitoring feed will move to Mosaic’s system
                when Harbor’s current service ends at close. An incomplete change
                could create a gap in required monitoring.
              parent_issue_id: null

            questions:
            - question_id: Q-SAR
              text: Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last
                year been reviewed, and what did they reveal?
              consequence: Unread open alerts and SARs are the highest-risk item;
                they can create BSA/AML exposure that must be addressed before close
                and could affect the deal itself.
              state: answered
              answer: The open alerts and SAR history have not been reviewed and remain
                in diligence.
              answer_kind: reported_fact
              linked_fact_ids:
              - FACT-20260909-070aec
            - question_id: Q-KYC
              text: For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents,
                what is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay's own BSA/AML customer identification
                and recordkeeping obligations?
              consequence: Whether the missing underlying documents create a compliance
                gap depends on how Mosaic plans to satisfy its own CIP/recordkeeping
                obligations for these users.
              state: answered
              answer: It is not yet known whether Mosaic Relay's AML/CIP program permits
                reliance on Harbor's prior KYC; compliance must confirm.
              answer_kind: reported_fact
              linked_fact_ids:
              - FACT-20260909-620c62
            - question_id: Q-MTL
              text: For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint,
                what is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval
                before onboarding those customers?
              consequence: Whether the four new markets can be served at close depends
                on license transferability and state approval, which is a gating regulatory
                question.
              state: answered
              answer: Mosaic Relay currently plans to use or assume Harbor's licenses
                for the four new markets.
              answer_kind: reported_fact
              linked_fact_ids:
              - FACT-20260909-771ee1
            - question_id: Q-BONUS
              text: How is the $50 welcome bonus structured?
              consequence: The structure determines whether the bonus triggers consumer
                disclosure, funds-flow, or state promotional requirements.
              state: left_open
              answer: null
              answer_kind: null

          cutover can create immediate compliance and customer harm. A controlled
          delay preserves reversibility.

              passages: &id032
              - start: 0
                end: 3962
                text: '# Known Facts


                  - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10
                  weeks out).

                  - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                  into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account
                  and balance and full access to Mosaic''s product set.

                  - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d by
                  Harbor.

                  - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic
                  Relay holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new
                  markets.

                  - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic
                  has pass/fail results for everyone but not the underlying documents
                  for users onboarded before 2023.

                  - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
                  terminates at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction feed
                  at Mosaic''s engine on day 1.

                  - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on first
                  transfer, launching close+1.

                  - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from
                  the last year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

                  - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                  into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account
                  and balance.

                  - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users
                  were already KYC''d.

                  - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail
                  results exist for everyone but underlying documents are missing
                  for users onboarded before 2023.

                  - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
                  terminates at close; plan is to repoint the transaction feed to
                  Mosaic Relay''s engine on day 1.

                  - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from
                  the last year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

                  - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase
                  (Mosaic buys Harbor''s assets)

                  - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying
                  on another institution''s prior KYC without re-verification, or
                  is re-verification required? — Not sure / need to check with compliance

                  - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from
                  the last year? — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

                  - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does
                  Mosaic Relay plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or
                  apply for its own? — Use/assume Harbor''s licenses

                  - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents,
                  what is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer
                  identification and recordkeeping obligations? — It is not yet known
                  whether Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program permits reliance on Harbor''s
                  prior KYC; compliance must confirm.

                  - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last
                  year been reviewed, and what did they reveal? — The open alerts
                  and SAR history have not been reviewed and remain in diligence.

                  - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint,
                  what is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval
                  before onboarding those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans
                  to use or assume Harbor''s licenses for the four new markets.


                  ## Assumptions


                  - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses
                  and Harbor''s MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through
                  the acquisition without new state approval

                  - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy
                  Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying
                  documents

                  - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed
                  and validated before close without a monitoring gap

                  - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject
                  to state MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

                  - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter
                  in 41 states (per the request).

                  - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock
                  purchase, which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert
                  obligations transfer (structure not yet confirmed).

                  '
              source_version: 58b0379461c2b3d9c58807fff3ac3f7136d5aedd4f20022fc8be9eeb64cec409

                text: '# Issues and workstreams


                  - Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate
                  under the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor''s MTLs
                  transfer/survive the acquisition

                  - BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor''s prior KYC (with
                  missing underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic
                  Relay''s independent CIP/AML obligations

                  - SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage
                  Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability

                  - Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring
                  when the SaaS contract terminates at close

                  - Marketing compliance: the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state
                  money transmission or consumer protection implications

                  - Customer account, contract, and data-transfer rights <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-af341445a7af4c06
                  -->

                  - Open alerts, suspicious activity history, and acquisition diligence
                  <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-d22ea3957f21252a -->

                  - State money-transmission authority after the asset purchase <!--
                  issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-65ae94508dcda1bf -->

                  - Reliance on Harbor’s prior identity verification <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-30caa16a9234ccf2

                  - Transaction-monitoring continuity at cutover <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-1d13a6636b8fbe60
                  -->

                  - Purchase-agreement authority and risk allocation <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-29efc151650e76a2
                  -->

                  - Customer terms, privacy, data transfers, and welcome bonus <!--
                  issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-fcd3954739e05481 -->

                  '

            buys Harbor''s assets)

            - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying on another
            institution''s prior KYC without re-verification, or is re-verification
            required? — Not sure / need to check with compliance

            - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from the
            last year? — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

            - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does Mosaic
            Relay plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or apply for its
            own? — Use/assume Harbor''s licenses

            - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents, what
            is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer identification
            and recordkeeping obligations? — It is not yet known whether Mosaic Relay''s
            AML/CIP program permits reliance on Harbor''s prior KYC; compliance must
            confirm.

            - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last year
            been reviewed, and what did they reveal? — The open alerts and SAR history
            have not been reviewed and remain in diligence.

            - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint, what
            is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval before
            onboarding those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans to use or assume
            Harbor''s licenses for the four new markets.


            ## Assumptions


            - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses and
            Harbor''s MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through the acquisition
            without new state approval

            - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy Mosaic
            Relay''s own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying documents

            - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed and
            validated before close without a monitoring gap

            - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject to state
            MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

            - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter in
            41 states (per the request).

            - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock purchase,
            which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert obligations transfer
            (structure not yet confirmed).

            '

          available_excerpt: '# Issues and workstreams


            - Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under
            the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor''s MTLs transfer/survive
            the acquisition

            - BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor''s prior KYC (with missing
            underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay''s independent
            CIP/AML obligations

            - SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage Harbor''s
            ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability

            - Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring when
            the SaaS contract terminates at close

            - Marketing compliance: the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state money
            transmission or consumer protection implications

            - Customer account, contract, and data-transfer rights <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-af341445a7af4c06
            -->

            - Open alerts, suspicious activity history, and acquisition diligence
            <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-d22ea3957f21252a -->

            - State money-transmission authority after the asset purchase <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-65ae94508dcda1bf
            -->

            - Reliance on Harbor’s prior identity verification <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-30caa16a9234ccf2
            -->

            - Transaction-monitoring continuity at cutover <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-1d13a6636b8fbe60
            -->

            - Purchase-agreement authority and risk allocation <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-29efc151650e76a2
            -->

            - Customer terms, privacy, data transfers, and welcome bonus <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-fcd3954739e05481
            -->

          inputs:
            business_question:
              question_id: BQ-c9d7c39f6380eb60
              text: Does any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration need legal
                review before the Nov 15 close?
              revision: legacy:6abf4a45ae87313af8db04b89d546e0e1a1c6137341b3d3c0d159c66cf64d54c
            facts:
            - fact_id: FACT-20260909-182bcc
              text: Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10
                weeks out).
              source_ids:
              - REQ-20260909-283892
              origin: null
              verification_status: null
            - fact_id: FACT-20260909-551367
              text: Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                into Mosaic Relay's app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account
                and balance and full access to Mosaic's product set.
              source_ids:
              - REQ-20260909-283892
              origin: null
              verification_status: null
            - fact_id: FACT-20260909-9a0c61
              text: Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC'd by
                Harbor.
              source_ids:
              - REQ-20260909-283892
              origin: null
              verification_status: null
            - fact_id: FACT-20260909-33293c
              text: Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic
                Relay holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new
                markets.
              source_ids:
              - REQ-20260909-283892
              origin: null
              verification_status: null
            - fact_id: FACT-20260909-aea8ec
              text: Harbor's KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic
                has pass/fail results for everyone but not the underlying documents
                for users onboarded before 2023.
              source_ids:
              - REQ-20260909-283892
              origin: null
              verification_status: null
            - fact_id: FACT-20260909-073838
              text: Harbor's transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
                terminates at close; plan is to repoint Harbor's transaction feed
                at Mosaic's engine on day 1.
              source_ids:
              - REQ-20260909-283892
              origin: null
              verification_status: null
            - fact_id: FACT-20260909-19aebc
              text: Marketing wants a 'Welcome' campaign with a $50 bonus on first
                transfer, launching close+1.
              source_ids:
              - REQ-20260909-283892
              origin: null
              verification_status: null
            - fact_id: FACT-20260909-adf2cb
              text: Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and 'a handful' of SARs from
                the last year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.
              source_ids:
              - REQ-20260909-283892
              origin: null
              verification_status: null
            - fact_id: FACT-20260909-4c1fd8
              text: Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                into Mosaic Relay's app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account
                and balance.
              source_ids:
              - MSG-20260909-9835ba
              origin: null
              verification_status: null
            - fact_id: FACT-20260909-f2c49f
              text: Plan is no re-verification of Harbor's existing KYC; Harbor users
                were already KYC'd.
              source_ids:
              - MSG-20260909-9835ba
              origin: null
              verification_status: null
            - fact_id: FACT-20260909-13d4c1
              text: Harbor's KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail

              source_ids:
              - MSG-20260909-9835ba
              origin: null
              verification_status: null
            - fact_id: FACT-20260909-78d5cd
              text: Harbor's transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
